title: Shapiro spikes in driven quantum fluids
authors: Vijay Pal Singh, Ludwig Mathey, Luigi Amico
abstract: arXiv:2611.05477v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Periodic driving of a Josephson junction produces resonant transport signatures known as Shapiro spikes, conventionally described by effective circuit models. Here, we demonstrate Shapiro spikes in a neutral quantum fluid using simulations of a potential-biased atomic Josephson junction. The dc-current resonances follow the expected Bessel-function scaling, including the suppression and revival of individual resonances with increasing modulation strength. We uncover their microscopic mechanism by showing that the phase-winding frequency develops finite plateaus at integer multiples of the drive frequency. These phase-locked states are sustained by quantized-vortex nucleation and the associated $2\pi$ phase slips. Remarkably, within a locking plateau, the dc current and density transfer can reverse direction while the phase-winding frequency remains locked to the drive, giving rise to negative-mobility transport. Our results establish a microscopic link between vortex-mediated phase slips, Shapiro resonances, and anomalous transport in a neutral quantum fluid, revealing how quantized vortices convert resonant transport into phase-locked dynamics with negative mobility.
summary:
- Shapiro spikes appear in a neutral atomic Josephson junction, with dc‑current resonances scaling as Bessel functions of drive strength.
- Phase‑winding locks to integer multiples of the drive frequency through quantized‑vortex nucleation and 2π phase slips, creating plateaus.
- In a locking plateau the dc current and density transfer can reverse direction (negative mobility) while the phase‑winding remains locked.

title: Quasicrystals are Functionally Graded Materials
authors: Michael J. Landry, Dominic Bollettieri, Akhil Sadam, Denisse C\'ordova Carrizales, Mingda Li
abstract: arXiv:2611.05478v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quasicrystals exhibit long-range order without translational periodicity, posing challenges to compute their electronic properties. Here we show that a quasicrystal can be represented exactly as a periodic approximant with a spatially graded phason, establishing a connection to functionally graded materials. Building on this connection, we develop a controlled quantum theory of quasicrystals. We derive a state-dependent control parameter governed by the quantum metric of local Bloch states, determining when finite approximations are reliable. We further construct a Hamiltonian that correctly predicts Bragg gap positions, quasimomentum equivalence, and quasiperiodic eigenstates to all orders in phason strain within a finite Fourier window. We verify the theory numerically and propose a diffraction-based experimental test of the gap shift induced by phason strain. Our framework opens a route to predicting the electronic structure and functional properties of quasicrystals using methods developed for functionally graded materials.
summary:
- Quasicrystals mapped exactly to periodic approximants with spatially graded phason, linking them to functionally graded materials.
- Introduced a quantum‑metric‑based control parameter that dictates when finite approximations are reliable.
- Built a Hamiltonian that predicts Bragg gaps, quasimomentum equivalence, and quasiperiodic eigenstates to all orders in phason strain, verified numerically and testable via diffraction.

title: Resonantly interacting $2e/3$ anyons: a controlled microscopic theory of anyon superconductivity
authors: Qingchen Li, Pavel A. Nosov, Zhaoyu Han, Si-Yuan Chen, Taige Wang, Eslam Khalaf
abstract: arXiv:2611.05529v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a microscopic theory of anyon superconductivity that connects electronic interactions in a lightly doped Laughlin state to the universal physics of a resonantly interacting anyon gas. Using geometric quantization of Laughlin quasiholes, we derive the effective many-body Hamiltonian of dilute charge-$2e/3$ anyons, including their valley structure, dispersion, and statistical and short-range interactions, together with an explicit map between anyon and electron observables. This reduces the dilute many-body problem to a few parameters fixed by data computable from few anyon numerics. In analogy with resonant Fermi and Bose gases, we organize the dilute anyon problem around a two-body binding resonance and its relevant and marginal perturbations. For a three-valley gas of charge-$2e/3$ anyons, we identify a resonance whose long-distance theory is governed by an Aharonov-Casher anyon Hamiltonian whose magnetic field is the statistical Chern-Simons field and whose ground state is exactly solvable. Using the ground state wavefunction, we demonstrate Cooper-pair off-diagonal long-range order directly in electron coordinates and determine the pairing symmetry and vortex-lattice structure. The leading perturbations at the fixed point are a relevant pair detuning and a marginal three-body contact in the valley-singlet channel, which determine the compressibility and sound velocity. A repulsive three-body coupling is marginally irrelevant, allowing the fixed point to control a parametrically broad dilute regime near pair resonance, while attractive three-body interactions instead generate charge-$2e$ trimers. More broadly, our results show that binding thresholds between competing anyon composites host universal resonant regimes that are not captured by the lowest-energy anyon species alone, providing a new setting for controlled theories of anyon matter.
summary:
- Microscopic theory connects lightly doped Laughlin state to a dilute gas of charge‑\(2e/3\) anyons via geometric quantization.
- Effective Hamiltonian includes valley structure, dispersion, statistical and short‑range interactions; ground state is exactly solvable in an Aharonov‑Casher framework.
- Shows Cooper‑pair off‑diagonal long‑range order in electron coordinates, identifies pairing symmetry and vortex lattice, and pinpoints relevant detuning and marginal three‑body contact perturbations controlling compressibility and sound velocity.

title: Classification and Signatures of Dissipative Quantum Hall-Superconductor Junctions
authors: Evgenii Zheltonozhskii, Barak A. Katzir, Yuval Oreg, Erez Berg, Netanel H. Lindner
abstract:
arXiv:2611.05555v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fractional quantum Hall (FQH) edges with proximity-induced superconductivity can host parafermionic zero modes (PZMs), making them a promising platform for topological quantum computing. Recent experiments [G"ul et al., Phys. Rev. X 12, 021057 (2022)] measured the edge conductance from crossed Andreev reflection (CAR) between counter-propagating FQH edges separated by a narrow superconductor. The observed conductance was small and non-quantized, with two distinct behaviors: some states show temperature-independent conductance, while others show conductance that grows as temperature decreases. We explain these results by dissipation to sub-gap modes in the superconductor and present a phase diagram for the FQH-superconductor junction. We show that for Jain states, temperature-independent non-quantized conductance occurs only in the presence of an integer mode (such as at filling $
u=1\pm rac{1}{m}$, with odd $m\geq3$) strongly coupled to the dissipative channel. The predicted temperature trends qualitatively agree with the experiment, which shows temperature-independent conductance for $
u=2/3$ and integer states, but not for $
u=1/3$ and $
u=2/5$. We propose comparing $
u=4/3$ and $2/3$ to test the predicted influence of the relative chirality of integer and fractional modes.
summary:
- Dissipation to sub‑gap superconductor modes yields non‑quantized, temperature‑independent conductance in FQH–superconductor junctions.
- Phase diagram shows this behavior only when an integer mode (ν = 1 ± 1/m) couples strongly to dissipation, matching experiments for ν = 2/3 and integer states but not ν = 1/3, 2/
- Predicts chirality‑dependent conductance: comparing ν = 4/3 to ν = 2/3 should test the role of relative chir

title: Bypass Transition via the Non-Hermitian Skin Effect
abstract: arXiv:2611.05563v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-Hermitian skin lattices can directionally amplify propagating signals. Here we show that this amplification and nonlinear feedback together drive a bypass transition to self-sustained motion, familiar from shear flows. A finite local excitation can trigger sustained periodic or chaotic motion while the resting state remains linearly stable. We develop a return-map theory that predicts the triggering threshold, its scaling with directional gain, and the instability governing near-critical dynamics. The threshold decreases exponentially with chain length. Weak noise triggers sustained motion as well, with a characteristic ignition length that grows logarithmically as noise weakens at fixed observation time. Our work establishes a skin-effect route to bypass transitions, opening a new avenue for predicting and controlling nonlinear wave dynamics.
summary:
- Non‑Hermitian skin lattices amplify signals directionally, enabling a bypass transition to self‑sustained motion from a finite local excitation while the resting state remains linearly stable.
- Return‑map theory predicts an exponentially decreasing triggering threshold with chain length and scaling with directional gain; weak noise can ignite motion with a logarithmically growing ignition length.
- The work establishes a skin‑effect route to bypass transitions, offering a new framework for predicting and controlling nonlinear wave dynamics.

title: DefectSkills: Guiding AI agents through first-principles calculations for point defects in semiconductors and insulators
authors: Zhenkun Yuan, Yizhi Zhu, Geoffroy Hautier
abstract: arXiv:2611.05654v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: First-principles defect calculations can now be performed autonomously by AI agents, enabled by established computational methods and open-source Python toolkits. However, reliable and repeatable defect calculations require clear scientific and technical guidance that helps agents resolve ambiguities and avoid errors in calculation setup, execution, postprocessing, and analysis. Here, we present DefectSkills, a set of structured prompts that provides human-in-the-loop guidance to AI agents performing first-principles calculations of point defects in semiconductors and insulators using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP). The prompts encode human expertise and guide agents through unit-cell relaxation, electronic-structure and dielectric calculations, phase-stability and chemical-potential analysis, charged-defect supercell generation and calculations, finite-size corrections, formation-energy calculations and thermodynamic analysis, and data backup. By packaging this expertise as reusable agent skills, DefectSkills supports consistent workflow execution across agentic AI systems and reproducible defect calculations.
summary:
- Introduces DefectSkills, a set of structured prompts that guide AI agents in performing autonomous first‑principles defect calculations with VASP.
- Encodes expert workflow steps—unit‑cell relaxation, electronic structure, dielectric, phase‑stability, charged‑defect generation, finite‑size corrections, and formation‑energy analysis—into reusable agent skills.
- Enables consistent, reproducible defect calculations across AI systems by providing human‑in‑the‑loop guidance for setup, execution, post‑processing, and data backup.

title: Medial Model of Elastic Curve Contacts, from Clasps to Knits
authors: Kathryn Chain, Haoye Sun, Michael S. Dimitriyev
abstract: arXiv:2611.05688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Materials constructed from interlocking and tangled fibers are challenging to model and understand due in part to the complex interplay between fiber shape and contact mechanics. Much of our intuition about contact mechanics comes from the Hertzian description, which is based on interactions between convex bodies. However, fibers often form clasp shapes, which involve saddle-shaped contact surfaces; the ability for two interacting bodies to conform to each other along a saddle surface confounds many existing mechanical contact models. Following an observation that contact surfaces between fibers tend to look like minimal, constant mean-curvature surfaces, we seek to test this hypothesis and provide a direct link to geometric modeling methods. To do this, we leverage the medial axis transformation, which generalizes the notion of a Voronoi tessellation to generating curves and surfaces. Through computational studies on an orthogonal clasp and a simple knit structure, we find that the medial axis transformation provides a reasonable model for contact surfaces between identical curves. We also show that a generalization of the medial axis transformation based on radical Voronoi tessellations can be used to well-approximate contact surfaces between non-identical curves. We apply this ``radical axis transform'' to curves of different radii and demonstrate a trend for surfaces to adopt finite mean curvature. Our results may point the way towards more sophisticated geometric methods for modeling tangles.
summary:
- Medial axis transformation captures saddle‑shaped contact surfaces between interlocking fibers.
- Computational tests on a clasp and knit confirm the model’s realism for identical curves.
- Radical Voronoi (radical axis transform) generalizes the approach to non‑identical curves, showing finite mean‑curvature surfaces.

title: Exact Mirror-Parity Selection Rule for Electron-Phonon Coupling in Two-Dimensional Crystals
authors: Nicol\'as F. Barrera, Javiera Cabezas-Escares, Francisco Munoz, Carlos Cardenas, Julia Contreras-Garc\'ia
abstract:
arXiv:2611.05710v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The electron--phonon (e-ph) interaction underlies conventional superconductivity and plays a central role in transport and other many-body phenomena in solids. Here, we derive a symmetry selection rule for e-ph scattering in two-dimensional crystals possessing a horizontal mirror plane, $\sigma_h$. For electronic states of mirror parity $s_n(\mathbf{k})$ and $s_m(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q})$, and a phonon mode of parity $\chi_
u(\mathbf{q})$, we show that the e-ph matrix element $g_{mn,
u}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})$ vanishes identically unless $s_n(\mathbf{k})\,\chi_
u(\mathbf{q})\, s_m(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q})=+1$. The rule follows from the covariance of the phonon-induced deformation potential under $\sigma_h$, constitutes the $C_s$ case of the general group-theoretical selection rule for matrix elements, and partitions the e-ph interaction throughout the Brillouin zone into symmetry-allowed and symmetry-forbidden scattering channels. Consequently, mirror-even phonons couple electronic states of the same mirror parity, either even--even or odd--odd, whereas mirror-odd phonons couple only states of opposite mirror parity, for both intra- and interband processes. We illustrate the selection rule through first-principles calculations for the two-dimensional superconductor $\mathrm{Sc_2BCH_4}$, where mirror parity is well defined throughout the entire Brillouin zone and symmetry-forbidden matrix elements vanish up to numerical precision. We then extend the analysis to bulk $\mathrm{MgB_2}$, where the rule applies exactly only on mirror-invariant planes of the three-dimensional Brillouin zone. Moving away from these planes removes the exact mirror constraint and activates scattering channels that are symmetry forbidden when the mirror eigenvalues are well defined. Our results establish horizontal mirror symmetry as an exact and practical filter of e-ph scattering processes.
summary:
- Mirror‑parity rule: \(g_{mn,
u}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})
eq0\) only if \(s_n(\mathbf{k})\,\chi_
u(\mathbf{q})\,s_m(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q})=+1\).
- Even phonons couple same‑parity states (even–even or odd–odd); odd phonons couple opposite‑parity states (even–odd).
- First‑principles test on 2D superconductor Sc₂BCH₄ shows symmetry‑forbidden matrix elements vanish to numerical precision.

title: Interplay between Spin Stripes and Pairing Crossover in the Bilayer Hubbard Model
authors: Zixuan Jia, Xuelei Sui, Shijie Hu, Tianxing Ma, Haiqing Lin, Bing Huang
abstract: arXiv:2611.05840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whether $d$-wave or $s_\pm$-wave pairing prevails in the bilayer nickelate \ce{La3Ni2O7} remains unresolved, and how its observed spin order and magnetic excitations relate to the pairing mechanism is unclear. Here, we use finite-temperature determinant quantum Monte Carlo simulations of a minimal bilayer Hubbard model to investigate pairing competition at strong interlayer coupling, where intralayer and interlayer antiferromagnetic correlations have comparable strengths. We find that spin stripes develop spontaneously with increasing hole doping, accompanied by a crossover of the dominant pairing symmetry from $d$-wave to $s_\pm$-wave. The crossover tracks the changing relative strengths of the spin correlations, with the interlayer correlations overtaking their intralayer counterparts in magnitude. Concomitantly, the dynamical spin structure factor exhibits a momentum-dependent reorganization of the magnetic excitations, consistent with fluctuating spin stripes. Our results identify the structure of spin fluctuations as a key link between spin stripes and pairing competition, offering a minimal-model perspective for understanding \ce{La3Ni2O7}.
summary:
- Spin stripes appear with hole doping, triggering a d‑wave → s±‑wave pairing crossover.
- The crossover follows the shift of magnetic correlations: interlayer AFM overtakes intralayer AFM.
- Momentum‑dependent reorganization of the spin structure factor signals fluctuating spin stripes tied to pairing.

title: Field evolution of the multi-$k$ magnetic states in NdB$_4$ revealed by neutron diffraction
authors: D. Brunt, N. Qureshi, E. Chan, B. Ouladdiaf, G. Balakrishnan, D. D. Khalyavin, O. A. Petrenko
abstract: arXiv:2611.06526v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the magnetic states of the Shastry-Sutherland-lattice magnet NdB$_4$ using single-crystal neutron diffraction. We focus on magnetic fields applied along the tetragonal $c$ axis, which stabilise the fractional 1/5~magnetisation plateau. In the low-temperature phase below 4.9 K, the transition into the plateau state at approximately 12 kOe is marked by a change in the propagation vectors from $(1/5,0,-2/5)$ and its double $(2/5,0,1/5)$ to $(0,0,1/5)$ and $(0,0,2/5)$. At the transition from the plateau to a nominally `field-polarised' state near 33 kOe, all magnetic reflections associated with non-integer propagation vectors disappear, whereas reflections corresponding to the $\mathbf{k}=0$ component persist throughout the entire field range. We conclude that that the in-plane components survive even in the high-field phase and that the polarisation is, in fact, incomplete. The observed field dependence provides direct support for a description of NdB$_4$ in terms of two coupled magnetic instabilities: all-in-all-out order of the in-plane moments and a spin-density wave of the out-of-plane components.
summary:
- NdB₄ exhibits a 1/5‑magnetization plateau at ~12 kOe, marked by a shift of propagation vectors from (1/5,0,–2//(2/5,0,1/to (0,0,1//(0,0,2/.
- At ~33 kOe the plateau collapses; non‑integer‑k reflections vanish while k = 0 reflections remain, indicating incomplete field‑polarization.
- Data support two coupled instabilities: in‑plane all‑in‑all‑out order and an out‑of‑plane spin‑density wave.

title: Stability of energy gap of macroscopic quantum matter
abstract: arXiv:2611.06528v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In quantum many-body physics and quantum field theory, it is often assumed that gapped systems remain gapped under sufficiently weak local perturbations. However, to what extent this assumption holds is elusive, except for some special systems. In this work, we examine the stability of energy gap of macroscopic quantum matter that is only subject to two physically natural conditions, locality and translation invariance. We first show that in any spatial dimension, there are gapped local Hamiltonians with a unique ground state and an unstable gap, i.e., they become gapless under certain arbitrarily weak local perturbation in the thermodynamic limit. We then prove that for both spin and fermionic systems in one dimension, such Hamiltonians with an unstable gap must not only break translation invariance but also be fine-tuned. We further show that in any dimension greater than one, there are fine-tuned local translation invariant Hamiltonians with a unique ground state and an unstable gap. These results greatly sharpen our understanding of the fundamental problem of the stability of quantum phases of matter. We also discuss implications of our results on, for example, anyon superconductivity and higher-form symmetries.
summary:
- Shows gapped local Hamiltonians can become gapless under arbitrarily weak local perturbations in the thermodynamic limit.
- Proves that in 1D unstable gaps require broken translation invariance and fine‑tuning; in higher dimensions fine‑tuned, translation‑invariant Hamiltonians can also be unstable.
- Highlights implications for phase stability, anyon superconductivity, and higher‑form symmetries.

title: Hidden entropic order of emergent charges in a classical Amp\`ere spin liquid
authors: H. Diego Rosales, Emma M. Bizot, Flavia A. G\'omez Albarrac\'in, Pierre Pujol
abstract: arXiv:2611.06795v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical spin liquids are characterized by an extensive number of ground-state configurations. Coulomb spin liquids have, in this ground-state manifold, a divergence-free local constraint, which gives dipolar correlations and pinch points in the structure factor. Recently, models with a complementary ground-state constraint, defined by a zero-circulation constraint (Amp\`ere's law), have been proposed. While classical Coulomb spin liquids forbid emergent charges, their Amp\`ere counterparts leave the charges unconstrained. Here we study an Ising Amp\`ere model on the octochlore lattice. The ground states obey a Gauss law for an antisymmetric rank-two field, i.e., three coupled two-dimensional Gauss laws, which are expected to produce pinch points in the structure factor. Nevertheless, maximal charges, vertices with all six arrows in or out, spontaneously accumulate on one of the two sublattices of the cubic lattice, with disordered signs. This order has a purely entropic origin; it washes out the pinch-point singularities at large scales, produces no magnetic Bragg peaks, and coexists with an extensive entropy. The system enters into this sublattice long-range ordered state through a continuous transition in what seems to be the three-dimensional Ising universality class. Moreover, the state has no magnetic order; it is even under time reversal: it is a hidden, entropic order within the Amp\`ere manifold. Thus, a system whose Gauss law would predict an algebraic spin liquid becomes, through a non-magnetic ordering transition, a partially ordered short-range spin liquid. Our study is based on a combination of the constraint-vector theory, exact bounds and enumeration, and Monte Carlo, Wang-Landau, and parallel-tempering simulations.
summary:
- Ising Ampère spin liquid on octochlore lattice: ground states obey zero‑circulation Gauss law, predicting pinch‑point correlations.
- Maximal charges self‑organize on one sublattice with random signs, forming an entropic sublattice order that erases pinch points and produces no magnetic Bragg peaks.
- The transition to this hidden order is continuous, in the 3D Ising universality class, while preserving extensive entropy and time‑reversal symmetry.

title: Noise-Induced Topology in Chiral Quantum Walks
authors: Alexandre Chaduteau, Derek K. K. Lee, Frank Schindler, Abhinav Prem
abstract: arXiv:2611.05471v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Noise typically destroys quantum coherence and washes out transport phenomena that rely on interference. Chiral quantum walks are a case in point: a particle hopping on a lattice threaded by a magnetic flux can spread asymmetrically due to interference between paths, an asymmetry that noise is expected to erase. Remarkably, we find that the most ubiquitous noise -- random fluctuations of on-site energies (dephasing) -- instead renders this asymmetry topologically robust. The density profile develops a skewness that grows in time while its center stays fixed, and in a finite chain the late-time relaxation modes pile up at one edge: a skin effect lacking the drift of conventional non-Hermitian skin effects. With multiple sites per unit cell, the dephasing strength alone can cause a topological phase transition, reversing the asymmetry. On a flux ladder with noisy rung hopping, the noise causes a drift of rung coherences, a quantum ratchet with no classical counterpart. Underlying these effects, the noise-averaged dynamics is an interacting (generically non-integrable) Lindbladian that remains analytically tractable. The modes governing late-time relaxation are bound states of the noise-induced interaction and form a band with a point gap, absent both without noise and under postselection, whose winding number fixes the direction of the asymmetry. These effects are within reach of several experimental platforms, including synthetic lattices, superconducting qubits, and optical lattices.
summary:
- Dephasing noise turns chiral asymmetry into a topologically protected skewness, with density profile skew growing while the center remains fixed.
- Noise induces a non‑Hermitian skin effect: late‑time modes pile up at one edge without drift, and dephasing can trigger a topological phase transition that reverses the asymmetry.
- The noise‑averaged dynamics is an interacting Lindbladian whose bound‑state band has a point gap; its winding number fixes the asymmetry direction and enables a quantum ratchet on noisy flux ladders.

title: Chiral edge modes from lattice Chern-Simons theory
abstract: arXiv:2611.05663v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: It is shown that a level $k$ Abelian lattice Chern-Simons theory with continuum time and a spatial square lattice, which is a topological field theory on the latticized plane and torus, when quantized on a spatial cylinder reduces to chiral edge excitations, exactly localized on the two boundaries and carrying two commuting lattice versions of the level-$k$ $U(1)$ Kac-Moody algebra of opposite chirality. The algebras are represented on a Fock space in the noncompact theory and by a finite Weyl algebra in the compact one. We also observe that the theory has a natural framing of Wilson loops which exhibits the correct framing anomaly.
summary:
- Lattice Chern‑Simons on a cylinder produces chiral edge modes confined to the two boundaries.
- These modes realize two commuting lattice U(Kac‑Moody algebras of opposite chirality (Fock space for non‑compact, finite Weyl algebra for compact).
- Wilson loops admit a natural framing that reproduces the correct framing anomaly.

title: Rotated-Frame Determinant Discovery for Ground- and Excited-State Quantum Selected Configuration Interaction
abstract: arXiv:2611.05941v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum Selected Configuration Interaction (QSCI) constructs a variational determinant space from measurements of a prepared electronic state, but finite-shot sampling can repeatedly observe high-probability determinants, limiting efficient discovery of configurations important for an accurate selected-CI description. We introduce rotate--sample--unrotate (RSU) determinant discovery, in which the same state is sampled in complementary orbital frames and the observed rotated determinants generate a finite set of candidates in the canonical basis. The Hamiltonian is then diagonalized in an orthonormal selected-CI space without enumerating the full determinant space. State-targeted orbital frames are constructed from an initial selected-CI wavefunction and its external residual. For excited states, we combine RSU with the generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) to prepare target-specific sampling states. Candidate GQE circuits are evaluated by classical selected-CI diagonalization in finite sampled spaces, so the quantum procedure requires only state preparation and determinant sampling. For N$_2$, exact-state controls isolate the determinant-discovery effect: at the stretched geometry, residual-natural-orbital RSU reaches chemical accuracy with 5,000 shots, compared with 20,000 shots for conventional QSCI. The improvement persists with approximate GQE-prepared states and is also observed for target excited states. These results demonstrate improved finite-shot determinant discovery in QSCI for both ground and excited states.
summary:
- RSU samples a state in complementary orbital frames, rotating observed determinants back to the canonical basis to efficiently build a selected‑CI space.
- RSU is paired with GQE for excited‑state targeting; candidate circuits are classically vetted via selected‑CI diagonalization, requiring only state preparation and sampling on the quantum device.
- For stretched N₂, RSU reaches chemical accuracy with 5,000 shots versus 20,000 for conventional QSCI, and similar improvements hold for approximate GQE states and excited states.
